questions.q: Which equation represents Ohm's law?
questions.explain: Ohm's law says the voltage across a conductor is directly proportional to the current, V = I x R.
why_wrong: This divides current by resistance, which gives nothing physical.
Current is V / R, not the product V x R.
Resistance is V / I; multiplying V and I gives power.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of electrical resistance?
questions.explain: Resistance is measured in ohms, the volt per ampere.
why_wrong: Siemens is the unit of conductance, the reciprocal of resistance.
Henry is the unit of inductance.
Farad is the unit of capacitance.

questions.q: Ohm's law is obeyed by a metallic conductor only if which quantity is kept constant?
questions.explain: Resistance of a metal rises with temperature, so V/I stays constant only if temperature is constant.
why_wrong: If current were held fixed there would be no V-I relation to test.
If voltage were held fixed there would be no V-I relation to test.
Power changes with V and I; holding it fixed does not keep R constant.

questions.q: A 4 kohm resistor has 12 V across it. What current flows through it?
questions.explain: I = V/R = 12 V / 4 kohm = 3 mA.
why_wrong: This inverts the formula (R/V).
This multiplies V and R instead of dividing.
This subtracts R from V instead of dividing.

questions.q: Which of the following does NOT obey Ohm's law, i.e. has a non-linear V-I curve?
questions.explain: A diode's current rises exponentially with voltage, so V/I is not constant; the others are linear (ohmic) at constant temperature.
why_wrong: A resistor at constant temperature has a straight-line V-I curve.
Copper at constant temperature is ohmic.
Nichrome at constant temperature is ohmic.

questions.q: What does Kirchhoff's current law (KCL) state?
options: The algebraic sum of voltages in a loop is zero
The algebraic sum of currents at a node is zero
Total power in a node is zero
questions.explain: KCL states that the current entering a node equals the current leaving it, so the algebraic sum is zero.
why_wrong: That is Kirchhoff's voltage law, not KCL.
That is Ohm's law.
KCL concerns currents, not power.

questions.q: What does Kirchhoff's voltage law (KVL) state?
options: The sum of currents at a node is zero
Voltages around a loop sum to zero
The sum of resistances around a loop is zero
questions.explain: KVL says the rises and drops of potential around any closed loop add up to zero.
why_wrong: That is KCL.
That is Ohm's law.
KVL concerns voltages, not a sum of resistances.

questions.q: KCL is applied at which part of a circuit?
questions.explain: KCL deals with currents meeting at a junction, called a node.
why_wrong: Closed loops are where KVL is applied.
KCL is not limited to one resistor; it applies at junctions.
KCL applies wherever branches meet, not just at a source.

questions.q: Which pairing of law and conservation principle is correct?
questions.explain: Charge cannot accumulate at a node (KCL), and energy gained around a loop equals energy lost (KVL).
why_wrong: This reverses the two principles.
Momentum conservation is not behind either law.
Mass is not what KCL conserves, and KVL is about energy, not power.

questions.q: At a node, 5 A and 3 A enter and 2 A plus an unknown current I leave. Find I.
questions.explain: By KCL, in = out: 5 + 3 = 2 + I, so I = 6 A.
why_wrong: This adds the 2 A to the incoming current instead of subtracting.
This multiplies the currents, which KCL never does.
This takes 8/2, dividing instead of subtracting.

questions.q: Two resistors R1 and R2 are in series across V. The voltage across R2 is:
questions.explain: The same current flows through both, so each gets a share of V proportional to its resistance: V2 = V x R2/(R1+R2).
why_wrong: This is the voltage across R1, not R2.
This inverts the ratio and would exceed V.
The denominator must be the total resistance R1 + R2.

questions.q: The voltage division rule applies to resistors connected in:
options: a loop with no source only
questions.explain: In series the same current flows, so voltage divides in proportion to resistance.
why_wrong: In parallel the voltage is the same across each; current divides instead.
A voltage divider is a series arrangement, not specifically a bridge.
A divider needs a source to divide.

questions.q: In a series voltage divider, which resistor gets the largest voltage drop?
options: the one with the largest resistance
the one with the smallest resistance
questions.explain: V = I x R with the same I, so the largest R drops the most voltage.
why_wrong: The smallest resistance drops the least voltage.
Position in the chain does not matter.
Drops are equal only when the resistances are equal.

questions.q: A 10 V source feeds R1 = 2 kohm and R2 = 3 kohm in series. What is the voltage across R2?
why_wrong: That is the drop across R1.
That assumes an equal split, but R2 is larger.
This divides by R1 alone instead of R1 + R2.

questions.q: A 12 V source drives 1 kohm, 2 kohm and 3 kohm in series. What is the voltage across the 3 kohm resistor?
questions.explain: Total R = 6 kohm, so V3 = 12 x 3/6 = 6 V.
why_wrong: That is the drop across the 1 kohm resistor.
That is the drop across the 2 kohm resistor.
This ignores the other resistors, but they share the voltage.

questions.q: Two resistors R1 and R2 are in parallel and carry total current I. The current through R1 is:
questions.explain: In parallel the current through a branch is the total times the OTHER resistor over the sum.
why_wrong: This is the current through R2.
This inverts the ratio and exceeds I.
A product of resistances is not a divider ratio.

questions.q: The current division rule applies to resistors connected in:
questions.explain: In parallel the same voltage is across every branch and the total current splits.
why_wrong: In series the same current flows, so there is nothing to divide.
The rule needs branches that share both end nodes.
A single branch carries the whole current.

questions.q: In two parallel branches, the larger current flows through the branch with:
options: the same current in both always
questions.explain: With equal voltage, I = V/R is larger for the smaller R.
why_wrong: Larger resistance carries less current.
Wire length matters only through resistance.
Currents are equal only if the resistances are equal.

questions.q: A total current of 9 mA splits between 1 kohm (R1) and 2 kohm (R2) in parallel. Find the current through R1.
why_wrong: That is the current in R2.
This assumes an equal split, ignoring the resistor values.
This multiplies by R2 without dividing by the sum.

questions.q: A 12 mA current enters three identical 6 kohm resistors in parallel. Each resistor carries:
questions.explain: Identical branches share equally: 12/3 = 4 mA each.
why_wrong: That would be the whole current in each branch.
This divides by 2, as if there were only two branches.
This multiplies by 3 instead of dividing.

questions.q: A PN junction is formed by joining:
options: a p-type and an n-type crystal
a metal and an insulating oxide
questions.explain: A PN junction is the interface between p-type and n-type material in one crystal.
why_wrong: Two p-type pieces form no junction.
Two n-type pieces form no junction.
A metal-insulator contact is not a PN junction.

questions.q: The depletion region of a PN junction contains:
options: only free electrons and no ions
fixed ions with few free carriers
only free holes and no ions
a dense cloud of free carriers
questions.explain: Diffusing carriers recombine near the junction, leaving fixed donor and acceptor ions.
why_wrong: Free electrons diffuse out and recombine there.
Holes also diffuse across and recombine.
The region is 'depleted' of carriers, hence its name.

questions.q: The majority charge carriers in n-type semiconductor are:
questions.explain: Donor doping supplies extra free electrons, which are the majority carriers.
why_wrong: Holes are the majority carriers in p-type.
Protons are fixed in nuclei and do not conduct.
Ions are fixed in the lattice.

questions.q: When a PN junction is forward biased, the depletion region:
questions.explain: The forward voltage opposes the barrier potential, so the depletion region shrinks and current flows.
why_wrong: Widening happens under reverse bias.
Bias changes the width.
The region only shrinks, it does not always vanish.

questions.q: Which statement about a reverse-biased PN junction is NOT true?
options: A large current flows due to majority carriers
A small leakage current flows due to minority carriers
questions.explain: Reverse bias blocks majority carriers; only a tiny minority-carrier current flows.
why_wrong: That is true: reverse bias widens the region.
That is true: this is the reverse saturation current.
That is true: the barrier height is raised by the reverse bias.

questions.q: The approximate cut-in (knee) voltage of a silicon diode is:
questions.explain: Silicon diodes start conducting appreciably at about 0.7 V.
why_wrong: 0.3 V is the value for germanium.
1.5 V is well above the silicon knee.
5 V is not a knee value for silicon.

questions.q: The approximate cut-in voltage of a germanium diode is:
questions.explain: Germanium's smaller band gap gives a knee near 0.3 V.
why_wrong: 0.7 V is the value for silicon.
1.1 V is not a knee value; 1.1 eV is silicon's band gap, a different quantity.
3 V is far too high for a Ge knee.

questions.q: Which diode is designed to operate in the reverse breakdown region?
options: Tunnel diode only in forward bias
questions.explain: A Zener diode is built to break down at a sharp, stable reverse voltage and hold it.
why_wrong: A rectifier diode is damaged by breakdown.
Point-contact diodes are not meant for breakdown operation.
Tunnel diodes work in forward bias, not for reverse regulation.

questions.q: A silicon diode (0.7 V drop) is in series with a 5 V source and a 430 ohm resistor, forward biased. What is the current?
why_wrong: This ignores the 0.7 V diode drop.
This adds the diode drop instead of subtracting it.
This uses only the 0.7 V instead of the 4.3 V across the resistor.

questions.q: The reverse saturation current of a diode roughly doubles for every temperature rise of about:
questions.explain: Minority-carrier generation rises quickly with temperature; the standard rule is a doubling per 10 C.
why_wrong: 1 C is far too small a step for doubling.
50 C is too large; the current would grow far more than twofold.
100 C is much too large.

questions.q: A rectifier is a circuit that converts:
questions.explain: A rectifier uses diodes to pass current in one direction, turning AC into pulsating DC.
why_wrong: That is an inverter's job.
Changing voltage level is done by a transformer.
Boosting DC is a converter's job.

questions.q: How many diodes are used in a bridge rectifier?
questions.explain: A bridge rectifier uses four diodes in a bridge configuration.
why_wrong: One diode makes a half-wave rectifier.
Two diodes make a centre-tapped full-wave rectifier.
Six diodes are used in three-phase bridges.

questions.q: A half-wave rectifier conducts during:
options: both halves of each full cycle
questions.explain: With a single diode, only one polarity of the input passes.
why_wrong: That describes a full-wave rectifier.
It conducts on the half it is biased for, not just one peak.
It blocks the opposite half cycle.

questions.q: A full-wave rectifier is fed from 50 Hz mains. What is the ripple frequency of its output?
questions.explain: A full-wave rectifier produces two output pulses per input cycle, so ripple frequency is 2 x 50 = 100 Hz.
why_wrong: 50 Hz is the ripple of a half-wave rectifier.
25 Hz would arise by halving the frequency.
200 Hz would need four pulses per cycle.

questions.q: An ideal half-wave rectifier has peak input 10 V. What is its average DC output?
why_wrong: That is the average of a full-wave rectifier.
That is the RMS of the sine input, not the rectified average.
Vm/2 is not the half-wave average; the correct divisor is pi.

questions.q: A forward-biased diode (above cut-in) behaves like:
questions.explain: It conducts with only a small drop, like a closed switch.
why_wrong: An open switch is the reverse-bias behaviour.
A capacitor stores charge rather than acting as a switch.
An inductor stores energy in a magnetic field.

questions.q: A reverse-biased diode behaves like:
questions.explain: Only a tiny leakage current flows, so it is essentially an open switch.
why_wrong: A closed switch is the forward-bias case.
It does not supply energy.
A short circuit would carry large current.

questions.q: For a silicon diode to switch ON, the forward voltage must exceed about:
questions.explain: The forward bias must overcome the barrier potential of about 0.7 V for silicon.
why_wrong: 0.3 V is the germanium figure.
7 V is not the cut-in voltage of silicon.
A real diode needs the knee voltage, not just any positive value.

questions.q: A silicon diode is connected in reverse across a 5 V source in series with a 1 kohm load. The load current is approximately:
questions.explain: The diode blocks, so only nanoamp leakage flows and the load sees almost no current.
why_wrong: 4.3 mA would flow if the diode were forward biased.
5 mA would need an ideal conducting diode.
5.7 mA adds the diode drop wrongly and also ignores blocking.

questions.q: Which is a limitation of a real diode as a switch compared with an ideal switch?
options: it has zero reverse current at all temperatures
a forward voltage drop (about 0.7 V for Si)
questions.explain: A real diode drops about 0.7 V when ON and has small leakage when OFF.
why_wrong: An ON diode has low resistance, not infinite.
A diode needs correct bias to switch.
Reverse leakage exists and rises with temperature.

questions.q: The three terminals of a BJT are:
questions.explain: A BJT has an emitter, a base and a collector.
why_wrong: Source, gate and drain are MOSFET terminals.
Anode, cathode and gate are thyristor terminals.
Those are generic circuit terms, not BJT terminals.

questions.q: The two basic types of BJT are:
questions.explain: BJTs come as NPN or PNP depending on the doping sequence.
why_wrong: NMOS and PMOS are MOSFET types.
PIN is a photodiode structure.
JFET and MOSFET are different transistor families.

questions.q: Which region of a BJT is made thinnest and lightly doped?
questions.explain: A thin, lightly doped base lets most carriers pass through to the collector.
why_wrong: The emitter is heavily doped.
The collector is moderately doped and the widest.
A BJT has no substrate region in this sense.

questions.q: For a BJT in the active region, the junctions are biased as:
questions.explain: Active operation, used for amplification, needs EB forward and CB reverse.
why_wrong: Both forward is saturation.
Both reverse is cut-off.
That is the reverse-active mode, not normal operation.

questions.q: A BJT has current gain beta = 100 and base current 40 uA. What is the collector current?
questions.explain: IC = beta x IB = 100 x 40 uA = 4 mA.
why_wrong: This is off by a factor of ten in the conversion.
This is off by a factor of ten in the opposite direction.
That is the emitter current (beta+1) x IB, not IC.

questions.q: CMOS stands for:
questions.explain: CMOS combines complementary NMOS and PMOS transistors.
why_wrong: The first word is 'complementary', not 'common'.
It is not a memory or operating-system term.
'Controlled' is not part of the name.

questions.q: A CMOS gate is built using pairs of:
questions.explain: Complementary means n-channel and p-channel MOSFETs work as a pair.
why_wrong: NPN and PNP are BJTs.
CMOS gates use transistors, not diode-resistor logic.
JFETs are not the basis of CMOS.

questions.q: Why does a CMOS inverter dissipate very little static power?
options: Both of its transistors are always on
It is built without any transistors
It has a large resistor to ground
One of its two transistors is always off
questions.explain: With one transistor off, there is no DC path from supply to ground.
why_wrong: Both on would short the supply to ground.
The inverter is made from transistors.
No resistor is needed; the off transistor blocks the path.

questions.q: In a CMOS inverter, when the input is logic HIGH:
options: NMOS is ON, PMOS is OFF, and the output is LOW
PMOS is ON, NMOS is OFF, and the output is HIGH
both are ON and the output is LOW
both are OFF and the output is HIGH
questions.explain: A high input turns on the NMOS and turns off the PMOS, pulling the output to ground.
why_wrong: This is the input-LOW case.
Both on would create a supply-to-ground short.
Both off would leave the output floating.

questions.q: Which is NOT an advantage of CMOS technology?
questions.explain: CMOS is valued for LOW static power, so high static dissipation is not an advantage.
why_wrong: This is a real advantage of CMOS.
High noise immunity is a real advantage.
CMOS scales well, giving high packing density.

questions.q: RAM is a type of ______ memory.
questions.explain: RAM loses its contents when power is removed.
why_wrong: Non-volatile memory keeps data without power.
RAM can be both read and written.
RAM is semiconductor memory, not optical.

questions.q: RAM stands for:
questions.explain: Any location can be accessed in about the same time, hence random access.
why_wrong: 'Read Always Memory' is invented; the R means random.
'Rapid Access Module' is not the standard term.
'Registered Array Memory' is not the standard term.

questions.q: A DRAM cell stores a bit as:
options: charge trapped in a floating gate
questions.explain: A DRAM cell uses one transistor and one capacitor, whose charge must be refreshed.
why_wrong: Magnetic storage is used in hard disks.
Floating-gate storage is used in flash memory.
Light is used in optical media.

questions.q: Which statement correctly contrasts SRAM with DRAM?
options: SRAM is slower and needs refresh
SRAM is faster, needs no refresh
SRAM stores each bit on a capacitor
SRAM is cheaper per bit than DRAM
questions.explain: SRAM uses flip-flop cells, so it is faster, needs no refresh, but costs more per bit.
why_wrong: SRAM does not need refresh and is faster.
The capacitor-per-bit cell belongs to DRAM.
SRAM is more expensive per bit because each cell uses about six transistors.

questions.q: CPU cache memory is typically built from:
questions.explain: Cache needs high speed with no refresh, which suits SRAM.
why_wrong: DRAM is used for main memory.
Flash is too slow for cache.
Tape is far too slow.

questions.q: A solid-state drive has:
questions.explain: SSDs store data in semiconductor chips, so nothing moves.
why_wrong: Spinning platters are in hard disks.
Read heads are in hard disks.
Motors are in hard disks.

questions.q: SSDs mainly use which type of memory?
questions.explain: SSDs store data in non-volatile NAND flash chips.
why_wrong: SRAM is volatile.
Core memory is obsolete.
Optical discs are different media.

questions.q: Compared with an HDD, an SSD generally has:
questions.explain: With no head movement, SSD random access is much faster.
why_wrong: HDD latency is higher because of seek and rotation.
Seek time belongs to HDDs.
SSDs are more shock resistant.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT true of an SSD?
options: It has no moving parts at all
questions.explain: Spinning magnetic platters describe an HDD, not an SSD.
why_wrong: True: data survives power-off.
True: SSDs use flash cells.
True: SSDs are fully electronic.

questions.q: A flash memory cell stores a bit by:
questions.explain: Charge trapped on the floating gate changes the transistor's threshold voltage and stays without power.
why_wrong: That describes DRAM.
That describes a hard disk.
That describes optical discs.

questions.q: The TPU is an AI accelerator developed by:
questions.explain: TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit and was made by Google.
why_wrong: Intel does not make the TPU.
AMD does not make the TPU.
Samsung does not make the TPU.

questions.q: NPU stands for:
questions.explain: An NPU is a chip designed to run neural-network workloads.
why_wrong: Nothing like a 'Network Power Unit' exists as an AI chip class.
'Numeric Print Unit' is not a real chip class.
'Node Programming Unit' is not a real chip class.

questions.q: AI accelerators are optimised mainly for which operation?
questions.explain: Neural networks are dominated by large matrix multiplications.
why_wrong: Not a core workload for accelerators.
Compression is not what they are optimised for.
Disk scheduling is an OS task.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT an AI accelerator?
questions.explain: A router forwards packets; it does not accelerate neural-network math.
why_wrong: TPU is an AI accelerator.
An NPU is an AI accelerator.
Tensor Cores accelerate matrix math for AI.

questions.q: Why do many AI accelerators use low-precision numbers such as INT8 or FP16?
options: Higher throughput per watt, little accuracy loss
They always give mathematically exact results
They need much more memory per stored value
Every CPU instruction set requires them
questions.explain: Smaller numbers use less energy and memory, and inference tolerates it.
why_wrong: Low precision is approximate, not exact.
Lower precision needs less memory.
No CPU rule requires it.

questions.q: A sensor is a device that converts:
options: a physical quantity into a signal
questions.explain: Sensors measure physical quantities such as temperature or light and output electrical signals.
why_wrong: That would be a speaker.
That is a rectifier.
That is not what a sensor does.

questions.q: Which sensor is used to measure temperature?
questions.explain: A thermistor's resistance changes with temperature.
why_wrong: LDR senses light.
PIR senses infrared motion.
Ultrasonic senses distance.

questions.q: A PIR sensor is used to detect:
questions.explain: It detects changes in infrared radiation from moving warm bodies.
why_wrong: That needs a humidity sensor.
That needs a gas sensor.
That needs a Hall sensor.

questions.q: The resistance of an LDR (light dependent resistor):
questions.explain: Light creates carriers in the LDR material, lowering its resistance.
why_wrong: It falls, not rises, with more light.
Resistance changes with light.
Light is its main influence.

questions.q: An ultrasonic sensor receives an echo 10 ms after emitting a pulse. If sound travels at 343 m/s, the distance to the object is:
questions.explain: The pulse travels there and back, so d = 343 x 0.010 / 2 = 1.72 m.
why_wrong: This forgets that the time is for a round trip.
This halves twice.
This has a wrong power of ten.

questions.q: LAN stands for:
questions.explain: A LAN covers a small area such as a room or building.
why_wrong: 'Long Access Network' is not the term; LANs are local.
'Large Area Node' contradicts the local scope of a LAN.
'Linked Address Network' is not the standard expansion.

questions.q: An IP address is used to:
options: identify a host on a network
questions.explain: An IP address uniquely identifies a host on a network.
why_wrong: Storing files is done by storage devices, not addresses.
Amplifying signals is a repeater's job.
Disk encryption is a software feature unrelated to IP.

questions.q: In which topology are all nodes connected to a central hub or switch?
questions.explain: A star has a central device connecting every node.
why_wrong: A bus uses a single shared cable.
A ring connects nodes in a circle.
A mesh connects nodes to many others.

questions.q: Which device forwards data packets between different networks?
questions.explain: A router uses IP addresses to move packets between networks.
why_wrong: A repeater only regenerates signals.
A hub broadcasts to all ports.
A modem converts signals, but does not route.

questions.q: How does a WAN differ from a LAN?
options: A WAN covers a much larger area
A WAN works only without cables
questions.explain: A WAN spans cities or countries, while a LAN spans a small area.
why_wrong: It is the larger one.
WANs rely on routers.
WANs use cables, fibre and wireless links.

questions.q: An optical fibre carries information in the form of:
questions.explain: Information is sent as light signals through glass or plastic.
why_wrong: Electric current is used in copper cables.
Sound is mechanical.
Magnetic flux is not used.

questions.q: Light is guided in an optical fibre by:
questions.explain: Rays reflect at the core-cladding boundary through total internal reflection.
why_wrong: Diffraction spreads light.
Polarisation does not guide light.
The photoelectric effect releases electrons.

questions.q: Total internal reflection occurs when light travels from:
options: a rarer to a denser medium at any angle
a denser to a rarer medium above the critical angle
a denser to a rarer medium below the critical angle
one medium to an identical one
questions.explain: Both a denser-to-rarer path and an angle greater than the critical angle are needed.
why_wrong: TIR cannot occur going to a denser medium.
Below the critical angle part of the light refracts out.
No boundary means no reflection.

questions.q: In an optical fibre, the core has ______ refractive index than the cladding.
questions.explain: The higher core index allows total internal reflection at the boundary.
why_wrong: A lower core index would let light escape.
Equal indices give no guiding.
A refractive index cannot be zero.

questions.q: Single-mode fibre is preferred over multimode fibre for:
questions.explain: Its small core allows one mode, cutting dispersion over long distances.
why_wrong: Multimode is typical for short links.
Multimode is cheaper for short runs.
Fibres carry light, not power.

questions.q: Wireless communication transmits information using:
questions.explain: Radio and microwave signals travel as EM waves through space.
why_wrong: Copper wires are wired.
Fibre is a guided wired medium.
Not a medium.

questions.q: Which frequency band is commonly used by Wi-Fi?
questions.explain: Wi-Fi uses the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands.
why_wrong: 50 Hz is mains frequency.
2.4 kHz is far too low.
240 THz is about optical frequency.

questions.q: Which technology is meant for short-range wireless links of roughly 10 m?
questions.explain: Bluetooth is a personal-area technology with a typical range of about 10 m.
why_wrong: Satellite covers huge distances.
A macro cell covers kilometres.
Microwave relays cover tens of km.

questions.q: A Wi-Fi signal has frequency 2.4 GHz. Its wavelength in air is about (c = 3 x 10^8 m/s):
questions.explain: Wavelength = c/f = 3e8 / 2.4e9 = 0.125 m = 12.5 cm.
why_wrong: This has a decimal slip by a factor of ten.
This is a factor of ten too big.
That is c/f with 240 MHz instead of 2.4 GHz.

questions.q: Which technology allows contactless data exchange over a few centimetres?
questions.explain: Near Field Communication works over about 4 cm, e.g. contactless payment.
why_wrong: Wi-Fi covers tens of metres.
LTE is a cellular technology.
GPS receives satellite signals.

questions.q: A GPU typically has:
options: a few very complex cores only
questions.explain: GPUs use many small cores for parallel work.
why_wrong: That describes older CPUs.
Every processor has cores.
That describes CPUs.

questions.q: A CPU typically has:
questions.explain: CPUs have a small number of strong cores with large caches.
why_wrong: That describes GPUs.
CPUs have caches.
CPUs have general-purpose units.

questions.q: Which workload suits a GPU best?
options: a long sequential task with many branches
a massively parallel task like matrix products
questions.explain: The same operation applied to large data sets maps well to thousands of GPU cores.
why_wrong: Branch-heavy sequential work suits a CPU.
OS scheduling suits a CPU.
Interrupts are handled by CPUs.

questions.q: Which task is better suited to a CPU than to a GPU?
questions.explain: CPUs have strong single-thread performance and handle complex control flow.
why_wrong: Pixels are parallel, so GPUs excel.
Training is parallel, so GPUs excel.
Frames are parallel work, suited to GPUs.

questions.q: A CPU is generally designed to minimise ______ while a GPU is designed to maximise ______.
questions.explain: CPUs optimise single-task latency; GPUs optimise total work completed per second.
why_wrong: This reverses the two goals.
Power and clock speed are design constraints, not the core CPU-vs-GPU goals.
Cost and core count are not the defining design goals.

questions.q: A 24 V supply drives 1 kohm, 3 kohm and 8 kohm resistors in series. What is the voltage across the 3 kohm resistor?
questions.explain: Total R = 1+3+8 = 12 kohm, so I = 24/12 = 2 mA. The drop across 3 kohm is 2 mA x 3 kohm = 6 V.
why_wrong: Ignores the 8 kohm resistor, using 24 x 3/(1+3).
Uses 24 x 3/8, treating the 8 kohm resistor as the whole circuit.
Assumes the supply splits equally between two resistors.

questions.q: At a node, 8 mA flows in through wire 1, 3 mA flows out through wire 2, and 2 mA flows in through wire 3. A fourth wire carries the remaining current away from the node. What is its current?
questions.explain: By KCL, current in = current out: 8 + 2 = 10 mA in, 3 mA out through wire 2, so the fourth wire carries 10 - 3 = 7 mA away.
why_wrong: Adds all three currents without regard to direction.
Subtracts both 3 mA and 2 mA from 8 mA, treating the 2 mA inflow as an outflow.
Adds 8 and 3 and subtracts 2, treating the 3 mA outflow as an inflow.

questions.q: A 12 V battery and a 5 V battery are connected in one series loop with their positive terminals facing each other (opposing), along with a total resistance of 700 ohm. What is the loop current?
questions.explain: KVL around the loop: 12 - 5 - I x 700 = 0, so I = 7/700 = 10 mA. Opposing EMFs subtract.
why_wrong: Adds the EMFs (17 V) instead of subtracting for opposing sources.
Uses only the 12 V battery and ignores the opposing 5 V battery.
Uses only the 5 V battery's EMF.

questions.q: A 60 W, 240 V lamp (treat its operating resistance as constant) is connected by mistake to a 120 V supply. What power does it dissipate?
questions.explain: R = V^2/P = 240^2/60 = 960 ohm. At 120 V, P = 120^2/960 = 15 W. Power scales with the square of voltage.
why_wrong: Halves the power because the voltage is halved.
Ignores the change in supply voltage.
Divides the power by 8, applying a cube law instead of V squared.

questions.q: In a Wheatstone bridge, the top arms are P = 100 ohm and Q = 200 ohm, and the bottom arms are R = 300 ohm (under P) and S (under Q). The galvanometer shows zero deflection. What is S?
questions.explain: Balance requires P/Q = R/S, so S = Q x R/P = 200 x 300/100 = 600 ohm.
why_wrong: Inverts the ratio, using S = P x R/Q.
Adds Q and R instead of using the ratio.
Uses S = P x Q/R, pairing the wrong arms.

questions.q: A 10 V source feeds a node through 2 kohm, a 4 V source feeds the same node through 3 kohm, and a 6 kohm resistor connects the node to ground. What is the node voltage?
questions.explain: KCL at the node: (10-V)/2 + (4-V)/3 = V/6 (kohm). Multiplying by 6: 30 - 3V + 8 - 2V = V, so V = 38/6 = 6.33 V.
why_wrong: Takes the simple average of the two source voltages.
Weights the sources by resistance instead of conductance.
Ignores the 4 V branch's different series resistance and the load, taking half of 10 V.

questions.q: A 12 V supply feeds a divider of R1 = 10 kohm (top) and R2 = 5 kohm (bottom). A 10 kohm load is connected across R2. What is the output voltage?
questions.explain: R2 in parallel with the 10 kohm load = 3.33 kohm. Vout = 12 x 3.33/(10+3.33) = 3.0 V.
why_wrong: Uses the unloaded divider formula and ignores the load.
Places the load across R1 instead of R2.
Adds the load in series with R2 in the denominator.

questions.q: A 5 V supply feeds a 10 kohm fixed resistor on top and a light-dependent resistor (LDR) on the bottom. In darkness the LDR is 100 kohm. What is Vout across the LDR?
questions.explain: Vout = 5 x 100/(10+100) = 4.55 V. The larger resistance takes the larger share of the supply.
why_wrong: Takes the voltage across the 10 kohm resistor instead of the LDR.
Assumes an equal split between the two resistors.
Ignores the 10 kohm resistor, treating the LDR as the whole circuit.

questions.q: You need an unloaded 3.3 V tap from a 5 V supply using a two-resistor divider with total resistance 10 kohm. What should the bottom resistor R2 (across the output) be?
questions.explain: Vout/Vin = R2/(R1+R2) = 3.3/5 = 0.66, so R2 = 0.66 x 10 = 6.6 kohm and R1 = 3.4 kohm.
why_wrong: Calculates the top resistor R1 instead of R2.
Reads the output voltage in volts as the resistance in kohm.
Chooses equal resistors, which gives 2.5 V.

questions.q: Two dividers are connected across the same 10 V supply. Left: 1 kohm on top, 3 kohm below. Right: 2 kohm on top, 2 kohm below. What is the magnitude of the voltage between the two midpoints?
questions.explain: Left midpoint = 10 x 3/4 = 7.5 V; right midpoint = 10 x 2/4 = 5 V. The difference is 2.5 V.
why_wrong: Assumes the two dividers always give identical midpoints.
Halves the difference between the midpoint voltages.
Uses only the right divider's midpoint voltage.

questions.q: A 9 V source drives a divider with 6 kohm on top and 3 kohm on the bottom. What is the Thevenin (source) resistance seen by a load connected to the tap?
questions.explain: With the source shorted, R1 and R2 are in parallel: 6x3/(6+3) = 2 kohm. The open-circuit tap voltage is 3 V.
why_wrong: Adds the resistors as if in series.
Takes the average of the two resistors.
Takes only the lower resistor.

questions.q: A 9 mA current enters a parallel pair of 6 kohm and 3 kohm resistors. What current flows through the 6 kohm resistor?
questions.explain: I(6k) = 9 x 3/(6+3) = 3 mA. The smaller resistance carries the larger current (6 mA).
why_wrong: Swaps the branches, giving the 3 kohm branch's current.
Assumes the current splits equally.
Divides 9 mA by 6 directly.

questions.q: A total of 22 A divides among three parallel resistors of 12 ohm, 6 ohm and 4 ohm. What current flows in the 4 ohm branch?
why_wrong: Assumes the current is shared equally by the three branches.
Uses 22 x 4/(12+6+4), treating them as series.
Gives the 12 ohm branch's current instead.

questions.q: A moving-coil meter has Rg = 100 ohm and full-scale current 1 mA. To make it read 10 mA full scale, what shunt resistance is needed?
questions.explain: The shunt carries 9 mA at the same voltage as the meter: Rsh = Ig x Rg/(I - Ig) = 1 x 100/9 = 11.1 ohm.
why_wrong: Uses Rg x Ig/I = 100 x 1/10, forgetting the meter's own current.
Divides by 11, using (I + Ig) as the shunt current.
Uses Rg x (n - 1), the series multiplier formula.

questions.q: A 20 V source is in series with an 8 ohm resistor, which feeds a 10 ohm and 40 ohm pair in parallel. What current flows through the 40 ohm resistor?
questions.explain: Parallel pair = 8 ohm, so total R = 16 ohm and I = 1.25 A. I(40 ohm) = 1.25 x 10/(10+40) = 0.25 A.
why_wrong: Swaps the branches, giving the 10 ohm resistor's current.
Applies 20 V directly across the 40 ohm resistor.
Reports the total circuit current.

questions.q: A 2 ohm and an 8 ohm resistor are connected in parallel across an ideal source. What is the ratio of power dissipated in the 2 ohm to that in the 8 ohm?
questions.explain: Same V, so P = V^2/R: the ratio is 8/2 = 4. Check: currents are in ratio 4:1, so I^2 R gives 16 x 2 : 1 x 8 = 4 : 1.
why_wrong: Squares the current ratio but forgets to weight by resistance.
Inverts the ratio.
Takes the square root of the ratio.

questions.q: At 300 K, an ideal Si diode (n = 1, Shockley equation) has its forward voltage raised by 60 mV in the exponential region. By what factor does the current rise?
questions.explain: VT = kT/e = 0.02585 V. The factor is exp(0.060/0.02585) = exp(2.32) = 10.2, roughly one decade per 60 mV.
why_wrong: Takes the exponent V/VT = 2.32 as the factor itself.
Evaluates exp(0.06) without dividing by VT.
Assumes 60 mV per decade applies twice.

questions.q: A Si diode has a reverse saturation current of 2 nA at 25 C, which doubles for every 10 C rise. What is it at 65 C?
questions.explain: The rise of 40 C gives 4 doublings: 2 x 2^4 = 32 nA.
why_wrong: Applies only two doublings.
Applies only three doublings.
Applies five doublings.

questions.q: A Si diode drops 0.70 V at 25 C at a fixed current. Taking the forward drop to fall by 2 mV per C, what is the drop at 75 C?
questions.explain: Delta T = 50 C, so change = -2 mV x 50 = -100 mV. The drop becomes 0.70 - 0.10 = 0.60 V.
why_wrong: Gets the sign wrong and adds the change.
Uses 1 mV per C instead of 2 mV per C.
Assumes the forward drop is independent of temperature.

questions.q: A 5 V source feeds 470 ohm in series with a parallel pair: a Ge diode (0.3 V) and a Si diode (0.7 V), both forward biased. What is the total current?
questions.explain: The Ge diode conducts first and clamps the node at about 0.3 V, so the Si diode stays essentially off. I = (5 - 0.3)/470 = 10.0 mA.
why_wrong: Uses the Si diode's 0.7 V drop for the whole current.
Adds the currents each diode would carry alone.
Subtracts both diode drops (1.0 V) in series.

questions.q: Which pairing correctly describes Zener and avalanche breakdown in a reverse-biased PN junction?
options: Avalanche: heavy doping, narrow depletion, negative temperature coefficient
Zener: light doping, wide depletion, positive temperature coefficient
Zener: heavy doping, narrow depletion, tunnelling, negative temperature coefficient
Avalanche: occurs only below about 3 V through field emission
questions.explain: Zener breakdown comes from field-assisted tunnelling in a heavily doped junction with a very narrow depletion layer, giving a negative temperature coefficient. Avalanche multiplication occurs in wider layers at higher voltages with a positive coefficient.
why_wrong: Avalanche needs a wider depletion region so carriers can gain energy; its coefficient is positive.
Reverses the characteristics; this describes avalanche.
Avalanche typically happens above about 6 V; field emission is the Zener mechanism.

questions.q: Which statement about an unbiased PN junction is NOT true?
options: Drift current exactly balances diffusion current, so net current is zero
Positive donor and negative acceptor ions are left uncovered in the depletion region
The barrier potential opposes the diffusion of majority carriers
A voltmeter across the diode terminals reads the barrier potential of about 0.7 V
questions.explain: The barrier potential cannot be measured with a voltmeter, because contact potentials at the metal-semiconductor junctions cancel it, so the net open-circuit voltage is zero. The other three statements are standard facts.
why_wrong: This is true: the equilibrium condition.
This is true: they create the built-in field.
This is true: it blocks majority carriers.

questions.q: A half-wave rectifier is fed from a 12 V rms secondary through a Si diode (0.7 V drop). What is the average (DC) load voltage?
questions.explain: Vp = 12 x sqrt2 = 16.97 V. Peak at the load = 16.97 - 0.7 = 16.27 V, so Vdc = 16.27/pi = 5.18 V.
why_wrong: Ignores the diode drop.
Uses the full-wave formula 2Vp/pi.
Treats the rms value as the peak value and ignores the drop.

questions.q: A bridge rectifier uses four Si diodes (0.7 V each) on a 12 V rms secondary. What is the average load voltage?
questions.explain: Vp = 16.97 V; two diodes conduct in each half-cycle, so the load peak = 16.97 - 1.4 = 15.57 V. Vdc = 2 x 15.57/pi = 9.91 V.
why_wrong: Ignores the diode drops.
Subtracts only one diode drop; two conduct at a time.
Applies the half-wave formula Vp/pi.

questions.q: A centre-tap full-wave rectifier uses a 12-0-12 V rms secondary (24 V rms end to end). Neglecting the diode drop, what peak inverse voltage must each diode withstand?
questions.explain: In a centre-tap circuit the off diode sees both halves in series: PIV = 2 x Vm(half) = 2 x 12 x sqrt2 = 33.9 V.
why_wrong: Uses only the peak of one half-winding.
Uses the end-to-end rms value.
Uses twice the peak of the full 24 V winding.

questions.q: In a two-input diode OR gate, inputs A = 5 V and B = 0 V drive the anodes of two Si diodes (0.7 V drop). Their cathodes join at the output, which has a resistor to ground. What is the output voltage?
questions.explain: The diode at the 5 V input conducts and the other is reverse biased. Vout = 5 - 0.7 = 4.3 V.
why_wrong: Ignores the forward drop of the conducting diode.
Adds the diode drop instead of subtracting it.
Takes the diode drop as the output.

questions.q: A bridge rectifier is fed from 50 Hz mains and supplies 10 mA to a load through a 1000 uF filter capacitor. Using Vpp = I/(f C) with f the ripple frequency, what is the peak-to-peak ripple?
questions.explain: A full-wave rectifier doubles the ripple frequency to 100 Hz. Vpp = 0.01/(100 x 0.001) = 0.1 V.
why_wrong: Uses 50 Hz as the ripple frequency, as for half-wave.
Halves the result by wrongly using 2 x f x C.
Treats the capacitor as 100 uF.

questions.q: A rectifier output has Vrms = 11.1 V and Vdc = 10.0 V. What is its ripple factor, and which circuit does it match?
questions.explain: Ripple factor = sqrt((Vrms/Vdc)^2 - 1) = sqrt(1.232 - 1) = 0.48. This matches the ideal full-wave value of 0.482 (half-wave is 1.21).
why_wrong: Takes Vrms/Vdc without subtracting 1 under the root, and mislabels it.
Quotes the half-wave ripple factor without calculating.
Computes (Vrms - Vdc)/Vdc, which is not the definition.

questions.q: An NPN transistor in the active region has base current 0.1 mA and beta = 50. What is the emitter current?
questions.explain: IC = beta x IB = 50 x 0.1 = 5 mA. IE = IC + IB = 5.1 mA.
why_wrong: Takes the emitter current equal to the collector current.
Subtracts the base current instead of adding.
Slips a decimal place in the calculation.

questions.q: A fixed-bias NPN circuit has VCC = 12 V, RB = 565 kohm to the base, RC = 3 kohm, beta = 100, and VBE = 0.7 V. What is VCE?
questions.explain: IB = (12 - 0.7)/565k = 20 uA, IC = 100 x 20 uA = 2 mA. VCE = 12 - 2 mA x 3 kohm = 6.0 V, so it is in the active region.
why_wrong: Assumes the transistor is cut off, so no drop across RC.
Subtracts a further 0.7 V from the result.
Assumes saturation, though IC x RC is only 6 V.

questions.q: An NPN switch drives an LED load of 1 kohm from VCC = 10 V. beta = 100, IB = 0.2 mA, and VCE(sat) = 0.2 V. What is the collector current?
questions.explain: beta x IB would demand 20 mA, but the load limits IC to (10 - 0.2)/1 kohm = 9.8 mA. The transistor is saturated and acts as a closed switch.
why_wrong: Applies beta x IB even though the transistor is saturated.
Adds VCE(sat) instead of subtracting.
Reports the base current.

questions.q: A transistor has alpha = 0.99 and base current 50 uA. What is the collector current?
questions.explain: beta = alpha/(1 - alpha) = 0.99/0.01 = 99. IC = 99 x 50 uA = 4.95 mA.
why_wrong: Uses beta = 1/(1 - alpha) = 100.
Multiplies the base current by alpha.
Uses beta = 98.

questions.q: Which combination gives a BJT a high current gain (beta)?
options: Lightly doped emitter, thick and heavily doped base
Heavily doped emitter, thin and lightly doped base
Equal doping in emitter and base, thick base
Lightly doped emitter, thin and heavily doped base
questions.explain: A heavily doped emitter injects many carriers into the base. A thin, lightly doped base lets most reach the collector before recombining, so IC is much larger than IB.
why_wrong: More recombination in the base loses carriers, lowering beta.
Poor injection efficiency and heavy recombination reduce beta.
The weak emitter injects few carriers while the base recombines them.

questions.q: Why does an idle CMOS inverter draw almost no static current, whereas an NMOS inverter with a resistor load draws current when its output is low?
options: Its PMOS and NMOS are both ON at once, so their currents cancel out exactly
The output node always floats at a voltage between the two supply rails
One complementary transistor is always off, so no DC path runs from VDD to ground
Its transistors have infinite resistance even while they are switched ON
questions.explain: For input high the NMOS is on and the PMOS is off, and vice versa for input low. There is never a steady conducting path, so only small leakage flows. The resistor-load version has a permanent path when the pull-down is on.
why_wrong: Both being ON would create a direct VDD-to-ground path.
The output is actively driven to a rail, not floating.
ON transistors have finite resistance; the key is that one is OFF.

questions.q: A CMOS chip's supply is lowered from 1.2 V to 0.9 V at the same clock frequency and switching activity. Its dynamic power becomes what fraction of the original?
questions.explain: Dynamic power = a C V^2 f, so it scales with V^2. (0.9/1.2)^2 = 0.5625 = 56.25 %.
why_wrong: Treats power as linear in supply voltage.
Applies a cubic dependence on voltage.
Reports the 25 % voltage cut as the remaining power, which is wrong.

questions.q: You are building a 3-input CMOS NAND gate. Which description of its network is correct?
options: 6 transistors: 3 NMOS in parallel to ground and 3 PMOS in series to VDD
3 transistors: one NMOS, one PMOS and one pass gate
4 transistors: 2 NMOS in series and 2 PMOS in parallel
6 transistors: 3 NMOS in series to ground and 3 PMOS in parallel to VDD
questions.explain: The output must go low only when all inputs are high, so the NMOS pull-down transistors are in series. The pull-up PMOS transistors are in parallel, so any low input pulls the output high.
why_wrong: This is the 3-input NOR arrangement.
A static CMOS gate needs a complementary pair for every input.
This is a 2-input NAND, not 3-input.

questions.q: A CMOS inverter input is slowly ramped from 0 to VDD. Where is the supply current largest?
options: At input = 0 V, where the NMOS is off and the PMOS is fully on
Near the threshold (about VDD/2), where both transistors conduct
At input = VDD, where the PMOS is off and the NMOS is fully on
It stays exactly the same value throughout the entire input ramp
questions.explain: At the extremes one transistor is off. Near VDD/2 both are in saturation, creating a brief direct path from VDD to ground. This is the short-circuit power component.
why_wrong: Only leakage flows here, since the NMOS is off.
Only leakage flows here, since the PMOS is off.
The current is near zero at the ends and peaks mid-ramp.

questions.q: What is latch-up in a bulk CMOS chip?
options: Gate-oxide breakdown caused by applying excess voltage to the gate
Output stuck permanently high because the transistor threshold voltage shifted
Slow output rise time caused by large interconnect wire capacitance
A parasitic PNPN thyristor triggers a low-resistance VDD-to-ground path
questions.explain: The p-substrate, n-well and source/drain diffusions form parasitic PNP and NPN transistors in a thyristor. If triggered by a transient, it conducts heavily between the rails until power is cut.
why_wrong: That is gate-oxide failure, which is a different mechanism.
Threshold drift is an ageing effect, not latch-up.
That is an interconnect delay, not a failure mode.

questions.q: In a balanced CMOS inverter designed for equal rise and fall times, why is the PMOS made wider than the NMOS?
options: The PMOS always has a higher threshold voltage than the NMOS by definition
Electrons have lower mobility than holes in silicon, so the NMOS is weaker
Holes are less mobile than electrons, so PMOS gives less current per width
A wider PMOS reduces static power consumption by cutting leakage current
questions.explain: Hole mobility in silicon is about two to three times lower than electron mobility. A PMOS of roughly 2-3 times the width gives matching drive current, so pull-up and pull-down delays are balanced.
why_wrong: Thresholds are set separately; the width follows from mobility.
It is the other way round: electrons are more mobile.
Width does not reduce static power; it increases capacitance.

questions.q: A CPU designer chooses SRAM rather than DRAM for the L1 cache. Which reason is correct?
options: SRAM is faster, needs no refresh, and uses a 6-transistor cell
SRAM packs more bits per area and costs less per bit than DRAM
SRAM stores each bit as charge on a small leaky capacitor
SRAM keeps its stored data even after the power is removed
questions.explain: An SRAM cell is a cross-coupled latch (six transistors) that holds its state without refresh and is read quickly. The extra area and cost are acceptable for small, fast caches.
why_wrong: DRAM, with one transistor and one capacitor per cell, is denser and cheaper.
That describes DRAM, which must be refreshed.
SRAM is volatile just like DRAM.

questions.q: How many address lines are required to address every byte of a 16 GB byte-addressable RAM?
questions.explain: 16 GB = 16 x 2^30 = 2^34 bytes, so 34 address lines are needed.
why_wrong: Allows only 4 GB of address space.
Uses the capacity in GB as the number of lines.
Allows 64 GB, which is more than needed.

questions.q: A TLC NAND flash cell stores 3 bits. How many distinct threshold-voltage levels must the controller distinguish?
questions.explain: n bits per cell need 2^n levels. For TLC, 2^3 = 8 levels, which is why TLC is slower and less durable than SLC.
why_wrong: Counts bits, not levels.
Doubles the bit count.
That is the level count for QLC, which stores 4 bits.

questions.q: A DDR4-3200 module has a 64-bit data bus and transfers on both clock edges. What is its peak bandwidth?
questions.explain: DDR4-3200 means 3200 mega-transfers per second. Each transfer moves 8 bytes, so 3200 x 8 = 25,600 MB/s = 25.6 GB/s.
why_wrong: Uses the 1600 MHz clock with no double-rate transfers.
Doubles the rate again, as if there were two channels.
Counts one byte per transfer instead of eight.

questions.q: Why can an SSD not overwrite a flash page in place, and what does this cause?
options: Pages cannot be read twice, so their data must be copied elsewhere first
Flash cells are volatile, so they need periodic refresh to keep their data
Erase works on whole blocks, causing garbage collection and write amplification
Writes are byte-sized while reads are block-sized, so mismatches occur
questions.explain: NAND is written in pages but erased in larger blocks. An update writes a new page and marks the old one stale, so the controller later runs garbage collection, which adds extra writes.
why_wrong: Flash pages can be read repeatedly without issue.
NAND flash is non-volatile; refresh is a DRAM feature.
Flash is written by page and erased by block.

questions.q: A first-generation TPU-style chip has a 256 x 256 systolic array of MAC units at 700 MHz. Counting each MAC as 2 operations, what is its peak throughput?
questions.explain: There are 65,536 MACs, each completing every cycle: 65,536 x 700e6 = 45.9e12 MAC/s. With 2 ops per MAC that is about 92 TOPS.
why_wrong: Counts each MAC as one operation.
Counts each MAC as four operations.
Misplaces the unit prefix by a factor of 1000.

questions.q: A 7-billion-parameter model in FP16 is quantised to 4-bit integers (ignoring scaling overhead). What is the weight storage afterwards?
questions.explain: FP16 uses 2 bytes: 7e9 x 2 = 14 GB. 4 bits is 0.5 byte: 7e9 x 0.5 = 3.5 GB, a 4x reduction.
why_wrong: This is the size at 8 bits per weight.
Assumes 2 bits per weight.
This is the original FP16 size.

questions.q: An edge camera runs object detection on a tiny NPU. Why do such accelerators typically use INT8 arithmetic instead of FP32?
options: INT8 is always more accurate than FP32 for every kind of neural network
INT8 operations need no memory access at all, unlike floating point ones
Lower energy, smaller multipliers, less memory traffic, little accuracy loss
FP32 numbers cannot be used for matrix multiplication on any hardware
questions.explain: Neural networks tolerate small rounding errors. INT8 multipliers are far smaller and use far less energy than FP32, and weights occupy a quarter of the memory, so more MACs fit in the same power budget.
why_wrong: FP32 has more precision; networks merely tolerate the reduction.
Weights and activations still have to be loaded.
FP32 works fine; it just costs more energy and area.

questions.q: How does bfloat16 differ from IEEE FP16?
options: It keeps FP32's 8-bit exponent, trading mantissa precision for range
It has more mantissa bits than FP16, giving it better precision
It uses a 5-bit exponent, like FP16, with a longer mantissa
It is an integer format that relies on a shared scale factor
questions.explain: bfloat16 has 1 sign, 8 exponent and 7 mantissa bits, so it covers the same range as FP32. FP16 has 5 exponent and 10 mantissa bits, so it has finer precision but narrower range.
why_wrong: bfloat16 has 7 mantissa bits, fewer than FP16's 10.
A 5-bit exponent is FP16's; bfloat16 uses 8.
It is a floating-point format, not integer.

questions.q: Generating tokens one at a time (batch 1) from a 14 GB model needs every weight read once per token. With 1 TB/s of memory bandwidth, what is the best-case token rate?
questions.explain: Each token requires moving 14 GB. At 1000 GB/s the limit is 1000/14 = 71 tokens/s, regardless of the compute available. The workload is memory-bandwidth bound.
why_wrong: Counts only half of the weights as read each token.
Uses the model size in GB as the rate.
Inverts the ratio.

questions.q: An NTC thermistor (top, to VCC) and a fixed resistor (bottom, to ground) form a divider whose midpoint feeds an ADC. As temperature rises, what happens to the ADC reading?
options: It falls, because the NTC resistance rises when the temperature goes up
It stays constant, because divider ratios do not depend on resistance
It rises: NTC resistance falls, so the fixed resistor takes more of VCC
It falls, because the fixed resistor's value drops as temperature rises
questions.explain: NTC resistance decreases with temperature. Vout = VCC x Rfixed/(Rntc + Rfixed), so a smaller Rntc raises Vout, and so does the ADC count.
why_wrong: An NTC's resistance falls as temperature rises.
The ratio depends directly on the resistance values.
The fixed resistor does not change.

questions.q: A 10-bit ADC with a 3.3 V reference measures a sensor output. What is the smallest voltage change it can resolve (1 LSB)?
questions.explain: A 10-bit ADC has 2^10 = 1024 steps. LSB = 3.3 V/1024 = 3.22 mV.
why_wrong: Uses an 8-bit ADC, dividing by 256.
Uses a 12-bit ADC, dividing by 4096.
Divides by 1000 instead of 1024.

questions.q: An ultrasonic sensor sends a pulse and receives the echo 11.66 ms later. Taking the speed of sound as 343 m/s, how far is the object?
questions.explain: The pulse covers the distance twice: d = v x t/2 = 343 x 0.01166/2 = 2.00 m.
why_wrong: Forgets that the pulse travels there and back.
Divides by 4.
Mis-converts milliseconds to seconds, using 0.0001 s.

questions.q: A 120 Hz vibration is sampled by an ADC at 200 Hz with no anti-alias filter. At what frequency does it appear in the data?
questions.explain: Nyquist needs fs > 240 Hz, but fs = 200 Hz. The signal aliases to |120 - 200| = 80 Hz, which is indistinguishable from a real 80 Hz vibration.
why_wrong: Assumes a correct reading even though fs is below 2 x 120 Hz.
Adds the signal and sampling frequencies.
Arises from no valid folding of 120 Hz about the 200 Hz sampling rate.

questions.q: A MEMS accelerometer lies flat and motionless on a table. What does its vertical axis read, and what does it read in free fall?
options: About 0 g at rest, and about +1 g in free fall
About +1 g at rest and also about +1 g in free fall
About 0 g at rest and also about 0 g in free fall
About +1 g at rest, and about 0 g in free fall
questions.explain: A MEMS accelerometer measures proper acceleration: the force per unit mass that acts on its proof mass. At rest the table pushes up, giving +1 g. In free fall nothing deflects the mass, so the output is about 0 g.
why_wrong: Reverses the two cases.
Gravity does not appear as a reading during free fall.
The sensor reports 1 g from the table's reaction force at rest.

questions.q: A 10 MB file (1 MB = 10^6 bytes) is sent over a 100 Mbps link of length 2000 km, with propagation speed 2 x 10^8 m/s. What is the total time to deliver it (transmission plus propagation)?
questions.explain: Transmission = 80e6 bits/100e6 bps = 0.8 s. Propagation = 2e6 m/2e8 m/s = 0.01 s. Total = 0.81 s.
why_wrong: Includes transmission delay but omits propagation delay.
Is smaller than the 0.8 s transmission time alone, so it cannot be the total.
Uses a 10 Mbps rate (ten times too slow) for the transmission time.

questions.q: A subnet is 192.168.10.0/26. How many usable host addresses does it provide?
questions.explain: A /26 leaves 6 host bits: 2^6 = 64 addresses. Subtracting the network and broadcast addresses gives 62 usable hosts.
why_wrong: Forgets to subtract the network and broadcast addresses.
This is the figure for a /25.
This is the figure for a /27.

questions.q: A live video-call app prefers UDP over TCP for its media stream. What is the best justification?
options: UDP guarantees in-order delivery of every packet, so nothing is ever lost
Late retransmissions are useless and TCP's retransmit delays stall the stream
UDP encrypts all of the data by default, which makes it far more secure
TCP cannot carry audio and video data at all, only plain text and files
questions.explain: In real time, a packet that arrives late is useless. TCP would hold back later data while waiting for a lost one, creating stalls; UDP lets the app skip or conceal the gap.
why_wrong: UDP offers no ordering or delivery guarantees.
Encryption is not part of UDP.
TCP can carry any bytes; the issue is latency.

questions.q: A path has 1 Gbps bandwidth and a round-trip time of 40 ms. To keep the pipe full, how much data must be in flight (the bandwidth-delay product)?
questions.explain: BDP = 10^9 bps x 0.04 s = 4 x 10^7 bits = 5 x 10^6 bytes = 5 MB.
why_wrong: Forgets to convert bits to bytes.
Uses the one-way delay, 20 ms, instead of the RTT.
Is a factor of ten too small; the bits-to-bytes conversion is applied wrongly.

questions.q: A host has address 192.168.1.130/26. What is the broadcast address of its subnet?
questions.explain: A /26 has blocks of 64 addresses: .0-.63, .64-.127, .128-.191. The host .130 lies in the third block, whose broadcast address is .191.
why_wrong: This is the first usable host address in the block.
This is the last usable host, one below the broadcast address.
This is the broadcast address of the whole /24.

questions.q: A step-index fibre has core index 1.48 and cladding index 1.46. What is its numerical aperture?
why_wrong: Takes the simple difference n1 - n2.
Forgets the square root.
Uses sqrt(n1^2 + n2^2).

questions.q: A fibre has attenuation 0.2 dB/km. A 1 mW signal travels 50 km with no amplifier. What power arrives?
why_wrong: Treats the 10 dB loss as a halving, as for 3 dB.
Treats 10 dB as a 10 % loss.
Treats 10 dB as a factor of 100.

questions.q: A Wi-Fi router transmits at 2.4 GHz. Taking c = 3 x 10^8 m/s, what is the wavelength of the wave?
why_wrong: Misplaces the decimal point by a factor of ten.
Corresponds to a frequency of about 3.75 GHz, not 2.4 GHz.
Misplaces the decimal point by a factor of ten the other way.

questions.q: In a step-index multimode fibre, what happens if the core-cladding index difference is increased?
options: The NA falls and the fibre then becomes a single-mode fibre
The NA rises and the intermodal dispersion falls as well
NA and acceptance angle rise, but intermodal dispersion grows too
Neither the NA nor the intermodal dispersion changes at all
questions.explain: NA = sqrt(n1^2 - n2^2) increases with the index difference, accepting more light. Steeper rays take much longer paths than axial rays, so pulse spreading grows and bandwidth falls.
why_wrong: A larger index difference raises the NA, not lowers it.
Larger delta spreads ray path times, increasing dispersion.
Both depend on the index difference.

questions.q: A 20 MHz wireless channel has an SNR of 30 dB. What is the Shannon capacity?
why_wrong: Uses 30 (in dB) directly as the spectral efficiency.
Uses SNR = 30 in linear terms, giving log2(31).
Uses an SNR of 15, i.e., log2(16)=4 bits/s/Hz.

questions.q: Which statement about single-mode fibre is NOT true?
options: Its core is wider than multimode's, so light couples more easily
Its core is only about 8-10 micrometres across, narrower than multimode
It has essentially no intermodal dispersion, as one mode propagates
It is normally driven by laser sources at 1310 or 1550 nm wavelengths
questions.explain: Single-mode fibre has a much narrower core (about 9 um) than multimode (50-62.5 um), so light is harder to couple. The other three statements are standard.
why_wrong: This is true: it is a very narrow core.
This is true: only one mode propagates.
This is true: those are the low-loss windows.

questions.q: Which workload would run better on a CPU than on a GPU?
options: Multiplying two large 4096 x 4096 dense floating-point matrices
Applying the same blur kernel to every pixel of a 4K frame
Computing a large batch of dense neural-layer activations
An interpreter full of data-dependent branches and pointer chasing
questions.explain: CPUs have strong branch prediction, large caches and fast single threads, which suit irregular, serial, branch-heavy code. GPUs shine when thousands of threads execute the same operation on different data.
why_wrong: Regular, data-parallel arithmetic favours the GPU.
Identical work on every pixel is ideal for a GPU.
Large uniform batches of arithmetic suit the GPU.

questions.q: 95 % of a program's runtime can be parallelised perfectly. What speed-up does Amdahl's law give on 64 cores?
why_wrong: This is the limit for infinite cores.
Multiplies 0.95 by 64.
Assumes perfect scaling of the whole program.

questions.q: A GPU has 5000 simple cores at 1.5 GHz, and a CPU has 8 cores at 4 GHz. If each core issues one operation per cycle, how many times higher is the GPU's peak operation rate?
questions.explain: GPU: 5000 x 1.5e9 = 7.5e12 ops/s. CPU: 8 x 4e9 = 3.2e10 ops/s. The ratio is 234.
why_wrong: Compares only the core counts.
Compares GPU throughput to a single CPU core.
Compares the clock rates and inverts the ratio.

questions.q: In a GPU warp, 32 threads run in lockstep and half take an if-branch while half take the else-branch. What is the effect?
options: Each half runs in parallel on its own separate warp scheduler unit
The branch has no cost at all, as the GPU predicts every branch perfectly
The warp stops and raises a hardware exception that the driver handles
Both paths run one after the other with half the threads idle each time
questions.explain: A warp issues one instruction at a time to all 32 lanes. With divergence, the if-path runs with the else-lanes masked, then the else-path runs with the if-lanes masked, doubling the time.
why_wrong: One warp executes one instruction stream at a time.
Prediction does not apply; the lanes must be masked.
Divergence is legal; it is only slower.

questions.q: Which feature is NOT characteristic of a GPU compared with a CPU?
options: Large per-core caches and deep out-of-order speculation for low latency
Thousands of lightweight cores that run very many threads at once
SIMT execution, where groups of threads share one instruction stream
Very high-bandwidth memory such as GDDR or HBM to feed many cores
questions.explain: The first option describes a CPU, which spends its transistors on cutting the latency of one thread. A GPU instead spends them on many simple cores that hide latency by switching between thousands of threads.
why_wrong: This is a GPU trait.
This is a GPU trait.
This is a GPU trait.
